doc.title: Henry Johnson interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Gospel and the blues as close cousins
summary: Woods asks how gospel shapes his playing; they agree gospel and blues say the same thing, one to God and one about a woman.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: You know I wanted to ask you a question, a couple of things here because you’ve got this marvelous mix and a lot of players I find have this mix. And it doesn’t get talked about that much in jazz history books, but you know, a lot of the jazz historians want to treat jazz as if it’s just jazz. But when I’ve talked to so many players, particularly to African American players that said, wait a minute, I got church background. I heard Gospel music when I was a kid, you know? Just give us an example of how the sound of the Gospel music goes into your playing — how that breathes some type of new life or conviction into your playing.

Well I think it is because the Gospel music is so closely linked with the blues. You know they talk about the same thing — give me a break. You know I mean how much blues can I take, how much, you know torment can I take, give me a break somebody. So in the Gospel music it’s give me a break, God, you know? And in the blues, give me a break period, somebody, you know?
One guy said it like this, he said the only difference between Gospel and rhythm & blues is one guy is talking about God and the other guy’s talking about his girlfriend.
The one guy’s talking about God loves me and he’s going help me, and the other one is talking about a woman left me and don’t care.
